stem: A 37-year-old day laborer presents with about nine weeks of progressive abdominal swelling and mild diffuse discomfort, which he attributed to weight gain from a recent change in diet. He has had intermittent low-grade fevers and reduced appetite. No prior TB treatment, no known TB contact, no known drug-resistant contact. Abdominal exam and imaging reveal moderate ascites with peritoneal thickening. Diagnostic paracentesis was performed; ascitic fluid was sent for molecular testing (along with biochemical and ADA testing), which returned positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: distended, mildly tender abdomen with shifting dullness, no peripheral edema, no jaundice.

patient.social_history: Lives with roommates; recent change in diet noted
patient.presenting_complaint: Progressive abdominal swelling, low-grade fevers, reduced appetite, initially attributed to weight gain
patient.exam_findings: Distended, mildly tender abdomen with shifting dullness, no peripheral edema, no jaundice, moderate ascites with peritoneal thickening on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever
comorbidities: mild, intermittent lower back discomfort, longstanding and unrelated

distractors: A recent change in diet proposed as sufficient explanation for the perceived weight/abdominal changes
A primary liver process proposed as the cause of the ascites, without pursuing diagnostic paracentesis first
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the ascitic fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the ascitic fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the ascites entirely to dietary changes and deferring diagnostic paracentesis and molecular testing
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
